title: Red Cliff Wells: Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Red Cliff wells have a 58 ft median depth, but fractured mountain bedrock makes yield and drilling cost vary widely.
intro_html:
Buying land near Red Cliff means dealing with mountain bedrock, limited well records, and large differences from one lot to the next. Colorado DWR records show 168 permitted wells within 5 miles, but only 51 are recorded as constructed. Of those, 58 report a total depth, 17 report a pump yield, and 5 report a static water level.

The records are useful for setting expectations, not for guaranteeing a result. Nearby wells in Minturn, Vail, Copper Mountain, and the surrounding Eagle County mountains can help a driller assess a site, but a new well still depends on the exact bedrock fracture system under the property.

sections.heading: Red Cliff well depth depends on fractured mountain rock
sections.html:
The recorded median well depth near Red Cliff is 58 feet. The middle half runs from 31 to 104 feet, and 71% of reported wells are under 100 feet. That gives a buyer a reasonable starting point, but it does not make a shallow well certain. The deepest well on record is 990 feet, and 3% of the depth records are 600 feet or deeper.

Fractured granite and gneiss can change quickly across a mountain parcel. A drill bit may encounter a productive fracture at modest depth or continue much farther through tight rock. For a drilling bid, ask for a per-foot rate and a clear explanation of casing, grout, mobilization, and what happens if the hole must continue beyond the planned depth.

sections.heading: Reported Red Cliff yields are strong, but the sample is small
sections.html:
Among the 17 wells reporting a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 15.0 to 85.0 gallons per minute, and 82% report more than 15 gallons per minute. No reported well is under 1 gallon per minute; 6% fall between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, while 12% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

Those figures are encouraging, but the yield data cover only a small part of the permit record. A pumping result is not the same as guaranteed household supply. Ask for the neighboring well yields, the test duration, recovery information, and the intended use. An exempt household-use well remains subject to its permit conditions and Colorado’s 35 gpm exempt-well pumping limit.

sections.heading: The Red Cliff water-level records do not show a clear trend
sections.html:
Only 5 wells near Red Cliff report a static water level, so the dataset is too limited for a reliable decade-by-decade trend. The median depth to static water is 50 feet, with the middle half between 12 and 65 feet. That describes the reported wells; it does not establish the water level on every lot or prove that groundwater is rising or falling across the area.

Static water level also changes with season, recharge, pumping, and local geology. Have the driller measure the new hole after construction and record the result. For an existing home, request the well permit, well construction information, pump details, and any recent production or water-level testing before relying on the well for a purchase.

sections.heading: Red Cliff permit activity spans several drilling eras
sections.html:
Permit records show activity near Red Cliff from the 1970s through the 2020s. The record includes 1 permit from the 1970s, 27 from the 1980s, 47 from the 1990s, 38 from the 2000s, 7 from the 2010s, and 27 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2022.

The most common driller names in these records are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 25 wells; Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Joe Wayne), with 19; and Steve Shelton Drilling, Inc. (Shelton, Steve), with 5. These records show who appears most often, not who is available now or best for a particular lot. Confirm current licensing, insurance, schedule, and references directly before signing a contract.

sections.heading: A Red Cliff well at median depth still has a full project cost
sections.html:
Red Cliff’s fractured mountain bedrock is commonly granite or gneiss. The drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 58-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $3,800 to $5,800. That is only the hole, not the complete water system.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is modeled at about $9,800 to $17,800 at the median depth. A deeper hole can raise both drilling and completion costs. Before comparing bids, confirm whether each proposal includes casing, grout, development, pump sizing, storage, electrical work, trenching, permitting support, and testing. Mountain access and the building site can also affect excavation and installation work.

sections.heading: Check mines, PFAS, septic, and dry-well risk before closing
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 247 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those entries do not automatically mean a particular well is contaminated, but they are reasons to review the property’s location, watershed, and prior land use. Test the finished well through a qualified laboratory, especially when a mine or cleanup site is nearby.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible in fractured bedrock even when nearby records look favorable. A home also needs suitable separation and layout for the well, septic system, access, and building foundation. Ask the county and Colorado DWR about setbacks, permit conditions, augmentation requirements, and wastewater approval before buying a lot. An over-appropriated basin may require an augmentation plan for the proposed use.

sections.heading: What to do before buying or building near Red Cliff
sections.html:
Start with the permit records for the exact parcel and then compare nearby wells toward Minturn, Vail, Copper Mountain, and other relevant mountain areas. Look for construction depth, reported yield, water level, use, and aquifer information, while remembering that all 168 records name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer and none name a Denver Basin aquifer.

For a purchase, make the contract contingent on reviewing the well permit, testing the water, confirming septic feasibility, and obtaining a contractor’s site-specific estimate. For a new build, have a licensed driller inspect access and propose a target depth, casing and grout plan, pump system, and testing program. Do not treat the 58-foot median or 15.0 gpm yield median as a promise for your lot.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Red Cliff, Colorado?
faq.a: The recorded median depth near Red Cliff is 58 feet, with the middle half between 31 and 104 feet. About 71% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Depth is not uniform in the fractured granite and gneiss, however. The deepest recorded well is 990 feet, so a driller should price work by the foot and discuss possible additional depth.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Red Cliff?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 58-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $3,800 to $5,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at about $9,800 to $17,800. Deeper drilling, difficult access, and site conditions can increase the final cost.

faq.q: How much water do Red Cliff wells produce?
faq.a: Among the 17 wells that report a pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute. The middle half is 15.0 to 85.0 gallons per minute, and 82% report more than 15 gallons per minute. This is a limited sample, not a guarantee. Request a pump test and recovery information for the specific well or neighboring wells.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Red Cliff?
faq.a: The permit map alone cannot establish that water is safe to drink. Within about 10 miles, records identify 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 247 historic mine features, and 6 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Have the well tested by a qualified laboratory for routine drinking-water concerns and site-specific contaminants before relying on it.

faq.q: Are there dry wells near Red Cliff, Colorado?
faq.a: The available records do not provide a dry-hole count. They do show substantial depth variation, from a 58-foot median to a deepest recorded well of 990 feet, in fractured mountain bedrock. That geology can produce sharp differences between nearby lots. Ask a local licensed driller to review neighboring wells, access, geology, and the property’s intended water demand.
